rationale: 'speak clearly' is an articulatory 'physical skill', but the part 'so others can understand you' is communication that the facet definition does not name.

'identify ... the speech of another person' matches 'classification' and the auditory perception of speech is 'sensorimotor intelligence', but 'understand' goes beyond what 'statistical pattern-matching' names.
'tell the direction from which a sound originated' is auditory spatial perception, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'focus on a single source of sound' is auditory perception under 'sensorimotor intelligence', but the attentional filtering of 'other distracting sounds' is not named in the definition.
'detect or tell the differences between sounds that vary in pitch and loudness' is auditory acuity, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'see objects in the presence of a glare or bright lighting' is visual perception, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'judge the distance between you and an object' is visual-spatial perception of one's surroundings, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'see objects or movement of objects to one's side' is visual perception, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'see under low-light conditions' is visual perception, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'match or detect differences between colors, including shades of color and brightness' is visual discrimination, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'see details at a distance' is visual acuity, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'see details at close range' is visual acuity, which 'sensorimotor intelligence' plainly covers.
'keep or regain your body balance or stay upright' is bodily balance control, plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'coordinate the movement of your arms, legs, and torso together' is whole-body motor coordination, plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'quickly and repeatedly bend, stretch, twist, or reach out with your body' is bodily movement, plainly 'physical skill'.
'bend, stretch, twist, or reach with your body, arms, and/or legs' is bodily movement, plainly 'physical skill'.

'exert yourself physically over long periods of time without getting winded' is physical, but it is cardiovascular endurance rather than the 'skill' or 'sensorimotor intelligence' the definition names.
'use your abdominal and lower back muscles to support part of the body' is physical, but it is muscular endurance rather than the 'skill' or 'sensorimotor intelligence' the definition names.

'exert muscle force repeatedly or continuously over time' with 'resistance to muscle fatigue' is physical, but it is muscular endurance rather than the 'skill' or 'sensorimotor intelligence' the definition names.

'short bursts of muscle force to propel oneself ... or to throw an object' is physical, but muscle force is a bodily capacity rather than the 'skill' or 'sensorimotor intelligence' the definition names.
'exert maximum muscle force to lift, push, pull, or carry objects' is physical, but muscle force is a bodily capacity rather than the 'skill' or 'sensorimotor intelligence' the definition names.
'quickly move the arms and legs' is motor performance, plainly 'physical skill'.
'fast, simple, repeated movements of the fingers, hands, and wrists' is motor performance, plainly 'physical skill'.
'quickly respond (with the hand, finger, or foot) to a signal (sound, light, picture)' links perception to movement, plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'time your movements ... in anticipation of changes in the speed and/or direction of a moving object or scene' is perception-guided motor timing, plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'choose quickly between two or more movements in response to two or more different signals' and start them 'with the hand, foot, or other body part' is plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'coordinate two or more limbs' is motor coordination, plainly 'physical skill'.
'quickly and repeatedly adjust the controls of a machine or a vehicle to exact positions' is precise motor control, plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'precisely coordinated movements of the fingers ... to grasp, manipulate, or assemble very small objects' is plainly 'physical skill'.
'quickly move your hand ... to grasp, manipulate, or assemble objects' is plainly 'physical skill'.
'keep your hand and arm steady while moving your arm or while holding your arm and hand in one position' is motor control, plainly 'physical skill'.

'shift back and forth between two or more activities or sources of information' is attention switching, which no facet definition, including 'sensorimotor intelligence' and 'plausibility auditing', describes.
'concentrate on a task over a period of time without being distracted' is sustained attention, which no facet definition, including 'sensorimotor intelligence' and 'plausibility auditing', describes.

'imagine how something will look after it is moved around or when its parts are moved or rearranged' is a what-if about an action, closest to 'intervention and counterfactual reasoning', but it is spatial imagery rather than causal reasoning.
'know your location in relation to the environment' and 'where other objects are in relation to you' is bodily spatial awareness, plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence'.

'compare similarities and differences among sets of letters, numbers, objects, pictures, or patterns' and 'comparing a presented object with a remembered object' are plainly 'pattern-matching' and 'retrieval'.
'identify or detect a known pattern ... that is hidden in other distracting material' is plainly 'pattern-matching' and 'classification'.
'combine, and organize information into meaningful patterns' matches 'pattern-matching', but 'make sense of' adds an interpretive step the definition does not name.
'remember information such as words, numbers, pictures, and procedures' is covered by 'retrieval' only in part, since storing information is not 'statistical pattern-matching'.
'add, subtract, multiply, or divide quickly and correctly' is exact arithmetic, which is not 'statistical pattern-matching' and is not named by any other facet definition.
'choose the right mathematical methods or formulas to solve a problem' is closest to 'problem formulation', but selecting a solution method is a poor match for that definition.
'combining or grouping things' matches 'classification', but 'generate or use different sets of rules' for grouping 'in different ways' goes beyond the definition.
'arrange things or actions in a certain order or pattern' is closest to 'pattern-matching', but following 'a specific rule or set of rules' is rule application rather than statistical matching.

'combine pieces of information to form general rules or conclusions' and 'finding a relationship among seemingly unrelated events' match 'statistical pattern-matching' and 'prediction' only in part, since forming general rules is broader than matching.

'apply general rules to specific problems' is logical deduction, which is neither 'statistical pattern-matching' nor 'causal structure', and 'answers that make sense' describes the output rather than 'plausibility auditing'.
'tell when something is wrong or is likely to go wrong' and 'only recognizing that there is a problem' is plainly 'plausibility auditing'.
'come up with ... ideas' is closest to 'generation', but 'unusual or clever ideas' and 'creative ways to solve a problem' are a poor match for 'statistical pattern-matching'.
'come up with a number of ideas about a topic' where 'the number of ideas is important, not their quality' is plainly 'generation' at scale.
'communicate information and ideas in writing' is covered by 'generation', but 'so others will understand' adds an audience aim the definition does not name.
'communicate information and ideas in speaking' is covered by 'generation', but 'so others will understand' adds an audience aim the definition does not name.
'read and understand information and ideas presented in writing' is closest to 'classification' and 'retrieval', but understanding ideas is a poor match for 'statistical pattern-matching'.

'listen to and understand information and ideas presented through spoken words and sentences' is closest to 'classification' and 'retrieval', but understanding ideas is a poor match for 'statistical pattern-matching'.
